justice: The road space is largely a single concrete carriageway without a dedicated sidewalk, so pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles must share the same narrow corridor.
The canal-side edge has only a low concrete wall and no separate protected pedestrian zone, indicating limited spatial allocation for slower and more vulnerable users.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or other barrier-free elements are visible along the lane, reducing accessibility for a broad range of users.
safety: The narrow lane forces mixed traffic between pedestrians, cyclists, and cars, increasing conflict risk because there are no lane markings or separated paths.
The canal runs directly along the right side of the road with only a low edge barrier, which provides limited protection against falls or vehicle runoff.
Utility poles and overhead wires line the roadway, while the route appears long and exposed with no visible street lighting infrastructure for night safety.
livability: The setting appears quiet and low-density, but there are very few visible active frontages, shops, seating areas, or public gathering spaces to support daily street life.
A police office is visible on the left, which may provide some civic presence, yet the overall street environment lacks amenities such as benches, shaded stops, or social spaces.
The canal and adjacent greenery add environmental presence, but the street itself functions mainly as a utilitarian access road rather than a vibrant shared public place.
sustainability: The canal and linear vegetation on the far side contribute some ecological value and open-space character within the corridor.
There is no visible bike lane, bus stop, or public transport facility, limiting support for low-carbon travel choices beyond basic walking and cycling.
Sparse street trees and minimal shade infrastructure reduce the street's climate resilience and green-streets performance despite the nearby water body.
aesthetics: The canal, open sky, and distant tree line create a relatively calm rural waterside view.
However, the exposed overhead utility wires and repetitive poles reduce visual neatness and skyline quality.
The building facades on the left show weathering and peeling surfaces, which lowers the overall visual maintenance standard of the streetscape.
comfort: There is almost no visible street tree canopy or shade structure along the road, so thermal comfort is poor under direct sun.
The concrete surface looks relatively even and continuous, which supports basic physical walking comfort.
No benches, resting points, or sheltered areas are visible, reducing comfort for people who need to pause or wait.
The road appears uncrowded and low-traffic at the moment, which likely improves psychological comfort through low noise and low congestion.
walkability: The paved surface is continuous and fairly flat, allowing straightforward walking along the lane.
Walkability is weakened because there is no dedicated sidewalk, forcing pedestrians to share the carriageway with vehicles.
The canal-side edge and absence of crossings, wayfinding, or pedestrian-focused elements make the route feel more like a vehicle access road than a pedestrian-oriented street.
bikeability: The road is narrow and has no designated bike lane or pavement markings to organize cycling space.
Cyclists would need to mix with cars in the same lane, which reduces perceived and actual riding safety.
No bicycle parking, repair facilities, warning signs, or intersection treatments for cyclists are visible, so cycling support infrastructure is minimal.
